problem: The premise contradicts itself. Changing ORG in the source 'without reassembling' changes nothing — the object file stays exactly as before, the code still sits at 2000H and JMP 2500H still works. The answer then explains what happens after a reassembly, so the question and answer describe two different situations. A student cannot tell which case is being asked.
fix: Rewrite the question for one clear case: 'A program is assembled with ORG 2000H and contains JMP 2500H, written as a fixed absolute address, not a label. You change the ORG to 3000H and reassemble. Why may the program now fail?' Answer: 'The bytes of the JMP operand are still 00 25, so the jump goes to 2500H. That address is now empty because the code moved to 3000H. Absolute addresses do not move with the program; only labels recomputed by the assembler move.'

problem: The node label 'Object .hex' joins two different file types into one name, while Section 2 explains that an object file and a hex file are not the same thing.
fix: Label the node 'Object file / hex file' or split it into two nodes.

problem: 'It has no labels, so a simulator shows addresses only' is too absolute. Most assemblers also emit a symbol or listing file that a simulator or debugger can load to show label names next to addresses.
fix: Say: 'The hex file itself has no labels, so on its own a simulator shows addresses only; loading the assembler's symbol file lets it show label names.'

problem: 'copied to the board by a programmer' can be read as a person rather than the device that burns the chip.
fix: Write 'by a device programmer (a hardware unit that writes the hex file into the chip)'.

problem: JNZ at 2003H is 3 bytes, so it occupies 2003H-2005H; a target of 2005H is the last byte of the instruction itself. The bytes asked for are correct, but the example makes a student picture a jump into the middle of an instruction.
fix: Use a target outside the instruction, for example 'JNZ at 2003H jumps to LOOP = 2010H. Bytes: C2 10 20.'
